Shared Domains: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) with a focus on Virtual Reality (VR)
Cognitive Neuroscience, particularly attention and brain activity measurement
Psychophysiology and the study of sickness symptoms in immersive environments
Method-Application Synergies: Psychology's dual-task paradigm and ERP analysis applied to Computer Science's VR environments to measure attention.
Computer Science's VR HMD technology used as a platform to induce and study psychological phenomena like VR sickness.
Psychological measures of attention (P3b ERP) used to assess the cognitive impact of VR sickness induced by specific VR path trajectories.
Complementary Technique Synergies: Electroencephalography (EEG) for brain activity measurement combined with Oculus Quest 2 HMD for VR immersion.
Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) for subjective symptom reporting integrated with objective P3b ERP amplitude measurements.
Multi-level modeling (MLM) and zero-inflated poisson (ZIP) regression for analyzing complex, repeated-measures data from EEG and SSQ.
Data-Method Synergies: EEG data collected during VR immersion analyzed using Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) to quantify attentional reserve.
SSQ scores and oddball counting errors analyzed with hierarchical linear modeling to understand relationships with P3b amplitudes.
Behavioral data (oddball count errors) and physiological data (P3b ERP) integrated to model the impact of VR sickness.
Cross-Domain Fusion Topics: Cognitive impacts of Virtual Reality sickness on attention and task performance.
Real-time tracking of attentional changes during immersive VR experiences using neurophysiological markers.
Development of novel methods for assessing cognitive function in VR environments.
Shared Application Areas: Improving user experience and effectiveness in VR training, education, and therapeutics.
Informing VR content development to mitigate negative cognitive impacts of VR sickness.
Neuropsychological assessments and therapies adapted for VR environments.
Joint Technique Development: Adaptation of EEG recording procedures for simultaneous use with VR HMDs, including artifact reduction strategies.
Development of a dual-task auditory oddball paradigm specifically for VR environments to measure attention during motion.
Modified ERP CORE package and EEGLAB software toolbox for VR-EEG data preprocessing and analysis.
Theory-Application Synergy: The theory of attentional capacity and reserve (Psychology) applied to understand cognitive resource depletion during VR sickness (CS application).
Sensory conflict theory of VR sickness (Psychology) informing the design of VR paths (CS) to elicit varying sickness levels.
Well-established P3b ERP component as a measure of attentional reserve (Psychology theory) used to dynamically track attention in VR (CS application).
Thinking Pattern Synergies: Psychology's focus on cognitive processes and human perception combined with Computer Science's expertise in immersive technology design and data analysis.
Empirical hypothesis testing from Psychology (e.g., sickness reduces attention) integrated with computational modeling from Computer Science (e.g., MLM, ZIP regression).
Rigorous experimental design from Psychology (e.g., dual-task paradigms, ERP analysis) applied to address practical challenges in VR user experience (CS).
Future Research Directions: Running a confirmatory follow-up study to further support the current results.
Adapting the dual-task oddball paradigm to compare attentional impacts across other VR applications.
Investigating the confound of VR sickness on other measures collected in VR.
Exploring real-time P3b tracking for dynamic assessment of attentional reserve in VR.
Summary Collaboration Themes: This collaboration fused Psychology's expertise in cognitive neuroscience and psychophysiology with Computer Science's VR technology to investigate the impact of VR sickness on attention. By combining EEG-based ERP measurements (P3b) with VR immersion and dual-task paradigms, they demonstrated that VR sickness significantly reduces attentional reserve and impairs task performance. This work provides a novel method for dynamically tracking attention in VR, offering crucial insights for designing more effective and comfortable immersive experiences in training, education, and therapy.
